reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: An infrequently traded corporate bond is quoted bid EUR 89.00, offer EUR 96.00.
ask: Its proportional bid-offer spread is closest to:

options.why: Decimal slip: 0.0757 is 7.6%, not 0.76%.
Scale slip (3×). Even dividing by half the mid only gets you to about 15%.
Units slip: EUR 7.00 is the dollar spread. Read as a proportion it becomes 7.0, or 700%.

takeaway: Proportional spread = (offer − bid) / mid. Illiquid bonds sit at about 5–10%.

reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: Normal market. An investor is short GBP 10,000 of stock A (proportional spread 0.030) and long GBP 17,000 of stock B (proportional spread 0.040).
ask: The cost of unwinding both positions is closest to:

options.label: ≈ GBP 49
options.why: Decimal slip: read the spreads as 0.3% and 0.4%, giving 15 + 34.

options.label: ≈ GBP 140
options.why: Netted the short against the long (7,000 × 0.04 / 2). Liquidity costs don't net: both legs must be traded.

options.label: ≈ GBP 1,500
options.why: Scale slip (3×). Even dropping the ½ only doubles it to GBP 980.

takeaway: Unwind cost = Σ sᵢ|αᵢ|/2, and longs and shorts add rather than net.

reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: Normal market. You have costed the long leg, GBP 17,000 of stock B at a 0.040 proportional spread: $0.040 \times 17{,}000 / 2 = $ GBP 340. The book also holds a short of GBP 10,000 in stock A (spread 0.030).
ask: Once the short leg is included, is the total unwind cost above GBP 340, below it, or about the same?

options.label: Below: the short offsets the long
options.why: That is market-risk thinking. Buying back the short also pays half a spread, so liquidity costs add.

options.label: About the same
options.why: The short leg costs GBP 150, nearly half of the long leg. It is not negligible.

takeaway: Diversification cuts market risk but not liquidity cost: every leg pays half a spread.

reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: CPR Bank holds 50 million shares quoted bid USD 80.40, offer USD 80.80, plus a commodity position with a mid-market value of USD 614m. The normal-market cost of liquidating the whole book is USD 12.0m.
ask: Is the commodity leg of that cost bigger than the shares leg, smaller, or about equal?

options.label: Smaller: the shares leg is most of the USD 12m
Bigger
options.why: Shares leg = units × dollar spread / 2 = 50m × 0.40 / 2 = USD 10m, so only USD 2m is left for the commodity.

options.label: About equal
options.why: The split is 10 : 2, not 6 : 6.

takeaway: Size the known leg first. The unknown leg is the residual, and here it is small.

reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: Stressed market, 95% ($\lambda = 1.645$). Shares: mid-market value AUD 1,400m, proportional spread mean 0.0340, SD 0.0180. Commodity: AUD 840m, mean 0.0044, SD 0.0044. Dollar-spread data are also on file (shares: mean AUD 1.0m, SD AUD 1.1m).
ask: The stressed cost of liquidation is closest to:

options.label: ≈ AUD 4.9m
options.why: That is the commodity leg alone. The shares leg (≈ 44.5m) dominates.

options.label: ≈ AUD 150m
options.why: Scale slip (3×). Even dropping the ½ only doubles it to about 99m.

options.label: ≈ AUD 2,000m
options.why: You used the dollar-spread rows as if they were proportions: 1,400 × (1.0 + 1.645 × 1.1) / 2 ≈ 1,970.

takeaway: Stressed cost = Σ (μ + λσ)α/2 on proportional spreads. The dollar-spread rows are bait.

reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: Hull's stressed-market liquidation cost is $\sum_i (\mu_i + \lambda \sigma_i)\,\alpha_i / 2$: each instrument's high-percentile spread is costed and the legs are summed. The book holds shares and a commodity.
ask: Compared with a model that lets the two spreads be less than perfectly correlated, this formula's figure is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Summing percentiles leg by leg assumes every spread blows out at the same time. Less than perfect correlation would diversify and lower the combined percentile.

options.label: The same
options.why: The two match only if the spreads really are perfectly correlated. With correlation below 1 the joint percentile is smaller, so the figures differ.

working.label: Built-in assumption
working.display: Summing $(\mu_i + \lambda\sigma_i)$ leg by leg = spreads perfectly correlated

working.label: Consequence
working.display: Any correlation below 1 gives a smaller joint percentile, so Hull's figure is an upper bound

takeaway: Stressed liquidation cost assumes spreads are perfectly correlated, so it errs on the high side. Hull defends this because spreads widen together when liquidity tightens.

reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: JCT Bank holds 1 million units each of a stock (mid value USD 72m) and a commodity (USD 47m). Dollar bid-offer spread per unit: stock mean 1.30, SD 1.03; commodity mean 1.32, SD 0.88. Stressed market, 99% ($\lambda = 2.326$).
ask: The stressed cost of liquidation is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 1.3m
options.why: That is the normal-market cost (means only): (1.30 + 1.32) × 1m / 2. The λσ term was dropped.

options.label: ≈ USD 11m
options.why: Scale slip (3×). Dropping the ½ gives only about 7.1m, and using 1.645 gives about 2.9m.

options.label: ≈ USD 210m
options.why: You multiplied the per-unit dollar spread by the position value (e.g. 1.30 × 72m). Dollar spreads multiply units, not value.

takeaway: With dollar spreads, multiply by units, not value. The price cancels.

reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: Stressed liquidation at 99% ($\lambda = 2.326$), 1 million units of each. Dollar spread per unit: stock mean 1.30, SD 1.03; commodity mean 1.32, SD 0.88. Each leg is units × (mean + 2.326 × SD) / 2.
ask: Which leg costs more to liquidate?

options.label: The commodity: its mean spread is higher
options.why: The commodity's mean is only 0.02 higher, but its SD is 0.15 lower, and at λ = 2.326 the SD term dominates: 3.70 vs 3.37 per unit.

options.label: Exactly equal
options.why: They differ by about 10%: USD 1.85m vs 1.68m.

takeaway: In a stressed cost, λσ usually outweighs μ, so rank legs on volatility of spread, not the average.

reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: 100,000 shares worth SGD 3.0m, quoted bid SGD 29.00, offer SGD 31.00. Daily volatility 1.43%, zero mean return, 99% ($z = 2.326$), constant spread.
ask: The one-day 99% liquidity-adjusted VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ SGD 20k
options.why: Scale slip (0.1×). Each leg is about SGD 100k on its own.

options.label: ≈ SGD 1.7m
options.why: You annualised the volatility (× √250), but the horizon is one day: 2.326 × 0.0143 × √250 × 3m ≈ 1.58m.

takeaway: LVaR = VaR + Σ sα/2. With a 6.7% spread, the liquidity leg is as big as the price leg.

reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: SGD 3.0m position quoted 29.00 / 31.00, constant spread. You have the one-day 99% market VaR: $2.326 \times 0.0143 \times 3.0\text{m} = $ SGD 99,785.
ask: The liquidity cost you add on is:

options.label: Much smaller (under a third of VaR)
options.why: A 2.00 spread on a 30.00 mid is 6.7%. Half of that on 3.0m is SGD 100,000.

options.label: Much bigger (over 3× VaR)
options.why: Half the proportional spread (3.3%) times 3.0m is 100k, about the same as VaR, not a multiple of it.

takeaway: Size the liquidity leg separately. For wide-spread assets it can match or beat market VaR.

reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: CNY 2.0m position quoted 39.00 / 41.00. The SD of the proportional spread is 2.0% and daily volatility is 2.00%. At 95% ($z = 1.65$ on both legs), market VaR is $1.65 \times 0.02 \times 2.0\text{m} = $ CNY 66,000. The spread is to be treated as volatile (stressed), not constant.
ask: Is the liquidity component bigger or smaller than the market VaR?

options.label: Smaller
options.why: With a constant spread you would get 0.05 × 2m / 2 = 50,000 < 66,000. The stated spread SD must be used: (0.05 + 1.65 × 0.02) / 2 × 2m = 83,000.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: 83,000 vs 66,000 is a gap of about 26%.

takeaway: A given spread SD tells you to use the stressed formula, and that can push liquidity above market VaR.

reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: BRL 1.0m position, expected return 14% p.a., volatility 26% p.a., one-year horizon, 95% ($z = 1.645$). Geometric returns are normal, so VaR $= V\,[1 - e^{\mu - z\sigma}]$.
ask: Compared with the normal-approximation figure $z\sigma V = $ BRL 427,700, the lognormal VaR is:

options.label: Larger
options.why: The lognormal form caps the loss below 100% and credits the 14% drift, so it comes in lower: about 250k.

options.label: About the same
options.why: At a one-year horizon the gap is large: 250k vs 428k.

takeaway: Over long horizons, lognormal VaR is well below zσV. Read 'geometric returns' as an instruction.

reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: BRL 1.0m position, volatility 26% p.a., one-year lognormal VaR at 95%: $V\,[1 - e^{\mu - 1.645\sigma}]$. The expected return is currently $\mu = 14\%$.
ask: If the expected return were 0% instead, the one-year VaR would:

options.label: Fall
options.why: A lower drift lowers the exponent, so the 5th-percentile value falls and the loss grows.

options.label: Stay the same
options.why: At a one-year horizon the drift matters: the exponent moves from −0.288 to −0.428.

takeaway: Higher expected return → smaller VaR. Over long horizons the drift is not negligible.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: ABC Bank: interest income USD 143m, interest expense USD 128m, total earning assets USD 950m, shareholders' equity USD 300m, cash USD 93m.
ask: The net interest margin is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip (0.3×). Bank NIMs live around 1–4%.
You divided by equity (15 / 300). Equity is funding, not an earning asset.
Gross interest income over earning assets (143 / 950): the expense was never netted.

takeaway: NIM = (interest income − interest expense) / earning assets. Bank NIMs sit around 1–4%, so a double-digit figure means you forgot to net.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: Davidson Bank reports a net interest margin of 2.45%, interest revenues of USD 100m and interest expenses of USD 64m.
ask: The earning assets it must hold are closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 15m
options.why: You divided 36 by 2.45 without converting the percent.

options.label: ≈ USD 150m
options.why: Decimal slip: you used 0.245 instead of 0.0245.

options.label: ≈ USD 4.1bn
options.why: Gross revenue divided by NIM (100 / 0.0245). The numerator is net.

takeaway: Earning assets = net interest income / NIM. Net in the numerator, decimal in the denominator.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: Total assets USD 1,212m, zero equity. Rate-sensitive assets USD 542m earn 5% and the remaining fixed assets earn 10%. Rate-sensitive liabilities USD 156m cost 4% and the remaining fixed liabilities cost 6%.
ask: Which block contributes more to net interest income: the rate-sensitive block (RSA income − RSL cost) or the fixed block (FA income − FL cost)?

options.label: The fixed block: fixed assets earn 10%
options.why: Fixed assets (670m) earn 67.0m, but fixed liabilities (1,056m at 6%) cost 63.4m, so the fixed block nets only about 3.6m.

options.label: About equal
options.why: It is 20.9m vs 3.6m.

takeaway: NII is a whole-balance-sheet quantity. The rate-sensitive block alone (20.86) is a trap answer.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: National Bank's cumulative interest-sensitive gap for the coming year is +USD 128m. Market rates are expected to fall by 1.5 percentage points.
ask: Net interest income over the year:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Sign slip: a positive gap helps only when rates rise. Here asset yields reprice down more than funding costs.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: Only a zero gap insulates NII. A positive gap is exposed to falling rates.

takeaway: Positive gap + falling rates → NII falls. The sign of ΔNII is the sign of gap × Δr.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: A bank's cumulative interest-sensitive gap is +USD 128m and market rates fall by 1.5 percentage points.
ask: The size of the change in net interest income is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.19m
options.why: You read 1.5 percentage points as 0.15% (0.0015).

options.label: ≈ USD 19m
options.why: You read 1.5 percentage points as 15% (0.15).

options.label: ≈ USD 190m
options.why: You multiplied by 1.5 without converting to a decimal.

takeaway: ΔNII = Δr (as a decimal) × gap. 1.5 pp = 0.015.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: A three-year USD 1,000 loan pays an 8% annual coupon and yields 8%, so it is priced at par. The present values of its cash flows are 74.07, 68.59 and 857.34.
ask: Its duration, compared with its three-year maturity, is:

options.label: Equal
options.why: Only zero-coupon or single-payment instruments have duration equal to maturity.

options.label: Longer
options.why: Duration is a PV-weighted average of the cash-flow times, and none of those times is later than year 3.

takeaway: Anything that pays cash before maturity has duration < maturity.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: A bond has duration 6.5 years and price USD 980. Rates on comparable bonds rise from 6.00% to 6.75%. Use $\Delta P / P = -D \, \Delta i / (1 + i)$.
ask: The size of the percentage price change is closest to:

options.why: Basis-point slip: you treated the 75bp move as 7.5bp (0.00075).
Scale slip (3×). Skipping the (1 + i) only nudges it to 4.9%.
You used the new rate level 6.75% instead of the 0.75% change: 6.5 × 0.0675 / 1.06 ≈ 41%.

takeaway: Duration × relative rate change: 6.5 × ~0.7% ≈ 4.6%. A 75bp move can't cost 41%.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: Duration 6.5 years; rates rise from 6.00% to 6.75%. You have the relative rate change: $\Delta i / (1 + i) = 0.0075 / 1.06 = 0.00708$.
ask: Is the bond's price loss bigger than 5%, smaller than 5%, or too close to call?

options.label: Bigger than 5%
options.why: 6.5 × 0.00708 = 0.046. Only a duration above about 7.1 would push it past 5%.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: 4.6% vs 5% is a clear gap. Even skipping the (1 + i) only gets you to 4.9%.

takeaway: Multiply duration by the relative rate change. Here the loss lands just under 5%.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: Green House National Bank: asset duration $D_A = 4.40$ years on assets of USD 648m, liability duration $D_L = 2.16$ years on liabilities of USD 401m. The unadjusted gap $D_A - D_L$ is 2.24 years.
ask: The leverage-adjusted duration gap is:

options.label: Smaller than 2.24 years
options.why: The adjustment multiplies $D_L$ by $L/A = 0.62 < 1$. That shrinks the amount subtracted, so the gap grows.

options.label: Equal to 2.24 years
options.why: It would be equal only if L = A (zero equity) or $D_L = 0$. Neither holds here.

takeaway: L < A, so the leverage-adjusted gap is always larger than D_A − D_L.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: Green House National Bank has asset duration 4.40 years, liability duration 2.16 years, assets USD 648m and liabilities USD 401m. Rates rise by 1 percentage point (ignore the $1 + r$ discount).
ask: Net worth:

options.label: Rises
options.why: A positive leverage-adjusted gap means assets lose more value than liabilities when rates rise.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: The gap is +3.06 years. That is far from immunised: ΔNW ≈ −3.06 × 648 × 0.01 ≈ −USD 20m.

takeaway: Positive leverage-adjusted gap → net worth falls when rates rise.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: Millennial National Bank: $D_A = 2.53$, $D_L = 0.65$, A = USD 367m, L = USD 219m. Rates rise from 5.0% to 8.5%. You have the asset leg: $-2.53 \times \tfrac{0.035}{1.05} \times 367 = -$USD 30.95m. The liability leg offsets part of it.
ask: Is the net change in net worth positive, negative, or too close to call?

options.label: Positive
options.why: The liability leg is only +4.75m (0.65 × 0.0333 × 219). It can't offset 30.95m.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The net is about −26.2m, far from zero.

takeaway: Short, small liabilities offset little. Net worth follows the asset leg down.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: A = USD 367m ($D_A = 2.53$), L = USD 219m ($D_L = 0.65$). Rates rise from 5.0% to 8.5%.
ask: The loss in net worth is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 2.6m
options.why: You treated the 3.5-point rise as 35bp (0.0035).

options.label: ≈ USD 67m
options.why: You used the new rate level (8.5%) in place of the 3.5-point change and dropped the (1 + r).

options.label: ≈ USD 260m
options.why: You read the 3.5-point rise as 0.35: 786 × 0.35 / 1.05 ≈ 262.

takeaway: ΔNW = −(D_A·A − D_L·L) × Δr/(1 + r). Check the size of Δr as a decimal before multiplying.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: Stress test: rates rise 300bp from 3.0%. Assets (USD m, duration): cash 75 (0), fed funds 130 (1), government securities and mortgages 160 (4), loans 240 (2). Liabilities: deposits 300 (0.5), borrowings 270 (3). Equity 35.
ask: The fall in net worth is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.85m
options.why: You read 300bp as 0.3% (0.003).

options.label: ≈ USD 2.8m
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×).

options.label: ≈ USD 36m
options.why: Asset leg only. The liability leg gives back about 28m.

takeaway: Shortcut: ΔNW = −(ΣD·A − ΣD·L) × Δr/(1 + r). Both legs are needed.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: ABC Bank: A = USD 180m ($D_A = 4$), L = USD 150m ($D_L = 3$), so net worth starts at USD 30m. Rates jump from 9% to 13%. Asset leg: −USD 26.42m. Liability leg: +USD 16.51m.
ask: After the shock, the bank's net worth is:

options.label: Negative
options.why: Even the asset leg alone (−26.42) leaves 3.6m of equity. The liability leg gives back 16.51, so ΔNW = −9.91 and NW ≈ 20.1m.

options.label: Too close to zero to call
options.why: That is the asset-leg-only slip: 30 − 26.42 = 3.6m. Add back the liability leg (+16.51) and NW ≈ 20.1m, about two-thirds of the starting equity.

takeaway: The duration formula gives a change. If the question asks for a level, add it back to the starting net worth.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: Harrier Bank: asset duration $D_A = 3.60$ years, assets USD 840m, liabilities USD 760m. It wants to immunise net worth by setting the leverage-adjusted duration gap to zero.
ask: The liability duration it needs is:

options.label: Equal to 3.60 years
options.why: That is naive matching, and it ignores that L < A.

options.label: Shorter than 3.60 years
options.why: Ratio inversion: $D_L = D_A \times A/L$, and $A/L > 1$.

takeaway: To immunise net worth, D_L = D_A × A/L, which is longer than D_A because fewer liability dollars must absorb the asset move.

reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: ABC Bank, 2019: high-quality liquid assets 1,458; average monthly withdrawals 2,458; expected 30-day net cash outflows under the stress scenario 1,700. (In 2018 HQLA was 2,100 against stressed outflows of 1,600.)
ask: In 2019, does the bank meet the liquidity coverage ratio requirement?

options.label: Yes: LCR is above 100%
options.why: Inverted ratio: 1,700 / 1,458 = 117%. LCR = HQLA / stressed net outflows.

options.label: Borderline
options.why: 86% is a clear breach, and it fell from 131% in 2018.

takeaway: LCR = HQLA / 30-day stressed net outflows ≥ 100%. Average withdrawals are bait.

reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: A trader unwinds a large illiquid position over $n$ days to minimise VaR after trading costs. The daily bid-offer spread widens with the quantity traded that day. At 95% confidence the optimal schedule front-loads, selling more than $V/n$ on day 1.
ask: If the confidence level in the objective is lowered (say to 75%), the daily amounts become:

options.label: More front-loaded
options.why: Front-loading is driven by price risk (the λσ term). A lower confidence means a smaller λ, so there is less reason to rush.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The schedule depends on λ. Hull's example flattens from 48.9 / 30.0 / 14.1 / 5.1 / 1.9 at 95% to 36.1 / 26.2 / 17.7 / 11.6 / 8.4 at 75%.

working.label: Comparative static
working.display: Lower confidence → smaller λ → the price-risk term shrinks → the schedule flattens. At 50% it is exactly $V/n$ per day

takeaway: Higher confidence → sell faster. Lower confidence → spread the unwind evenly.

reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: In a deleveraging cycle, banks cut credit lines and leveraged investors are forced to sell, which pushes asset prices down. Measured leverage is assets ÷ equity.
ask: As asset prices fall, investors' measured leverage:

options.label: Falls
options.why: Equity absorbs the price loss first, so the denominator shrinks proportionally faster than the numerator.

options.label: Stays the same
options.why: Assets and equity fall by the same dollar amount, not the same percentage, so the ratio moves.

working.label: Mechanism
working.display: Price fall → equity absorbs loss → assets/equity rises → further forced sales

takeaway: Deleveraging is self-reinforcing: falling prices raise measured leverage and force more selling.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: A lending institution runs the typical maturity profile: its loans and securities mature later than the deposits and borrowings that fund them. The yield curve flattens and then inverts, with short rates above long rates.
ask: Its net interest margin:

options.label: Widens
options.why: A positive maturity gap earns the long-minus-short spread. Flattening removes that spread.

options.label: Is unaffected
options.why: Borrow-short / lend-long profits depend directly on the slope of the curve.

working.label: Maturity gap
working.display: Asset maturity > liability maturity → positive maturity gap

working.label: Curve effect
working.display: Upward slope pays for the gap. A flat or inverted curve gives a small or even negative margin

takeaway: Positive maturity gap + flattening or inverting curve → NIM squeezed.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: Rate-sensitive items (USD m, sensitivity weight): fed funds loans 60 (1.00), investments 40 (1.30), loans and leases 150 (1.50); interest-bearing deposits 180 (0.86), money market borrowings 90 (0.91). The unweighted gap is $250 - 270 = -20$.
ask: The fed funds rate rises 2 points. Allowing for the weights, net interest income:

options.label: Falls
options.why: That is the unweighted reading (−20 × 0.02 = −0.40m). The weights flip the gap to +100.3.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: The weighted gap is +100.3m, so ΔNII ≈ +2.0m.

takeaway: Basis risk can flip the sign of the gap. Weight before you call the direction.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: Two bonds have the same maturity and the same yield. One carries a higher promised coupon rate.
ask: The higher-coupon bond's convexity is:

options.label: Higher
options.why: More coupon means more cash early, so duration is shorter and curvature is less. Convexity falls as the coupon rises.

options.label: The same
options.why: Maturity and yield are held fixed, but the coupon still changes the timing of the cash flows and so the curvature.

working.label: Rule
working.display: Maturity and yield fixed: higher coupon → lower convexity. Convexity also rises with duration

takeaway: Convexity rises with duration and falls with coupon.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: A bank estimates the change in value of a positively convex bond portfolio with the linear rule $\Delta P / P = -D\,\Delta i/(1+i)$. Rates then jump by 200bp.
ask: Relative to the true change, the duration estimate of the loss:

options.label: Understates the loss
options.why: The true price curve lies above its tangent line, so actual prices fall by less than the line predicts.

options.label: Is exact
options.why: The linear rule is only a first-order approximation, and its error grows with the square of the rate move.

working.label: Geometry
working.display: Positive convexity → the true price–yield curve lies above the tangent (duration) line on both sides

working.label: Rate rise
working.display: True price falls by less than the line → the estimate overstates the loss. For a rate fall it understates the gain

takeaway: Positive convexity: duration overstates losses and understates gains, and the error is bigger for bigger moves.

reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
setup: A USD 100 face Treasury bill is bought for USD 88 and matures in 120 days. Its bank discount rate is 36.00%, measured on a face-value base with a 360-day year.
ask: Its yield-to-maturity equivalent yield (purchase-price base, 365-day year) is:

options.label: Lower than 36%
options.why: Both conventions push the same way. The smaller base (88) and the longer year (365) each raise the figure.

options.label: Equal to 36%
options.why: The base and the day count both push the equivalent yield up, so for any bill bought at a discount the two can't coincide.

takeaway: The bank discount rate understates the true return: it uses the face-value base and a 360-day year.

reading: LR2025: Repurchase Agreements and Financing
setup: Traders' demand to short one specific government bond issue rises sharply relative to the supply available to borrow in the repo market.
ask: That issue's own repo rate, relative to the general collateral (GC) rate, moves:

options.label: Up, above GC
options.why: Polarity slip. Cash lenders compete to get the scarce bond and accept a lower rate on their cash.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Scarcity is priced through the repo rate. That is the special spread.

working.label: Mechanism
working.display: Scarce issue → cash lenders accept less interest to get it → repo rate falls

working.label: Special spread
working.display: GC rate − issue repo rate widens

takeaway: Going special means a repo rate below GC. More shorting demand → wider special spread → cheaper financing for the bond's owner.

reading: LR2025, Ch. 17: Liquidity Transfer Pricing
setup: A bank switches its liquidity transfer pricing from matched-maturity marginal cost of funds to a zero cost-of-funds approach, where business lines are charged nothing for liquidity.
ask: The maturity transformation on its balance sheet tends to:

options.label: Decrease
options.why: With liquidity free, long illiquid assets look more profitable and get funded with the cheapest, shortest money.

options.label: Stay the same
options.why: The internal price signal drives what business lines book. Removing it changes the balance sheet.

working.label: Ranking
working.display: Maturity transformation: zero cost > average cost > matched-maturity (none by design)

takeaway: The cheaper liquidity looks internally, the more the bank lends long and funds short.

reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
setup: Since 2008, covered interest parity has shown persistent deviations (a cross-currency basis). Banks shrink their balance sheets around regulatory reporting dates.
ask: As a quarter-end approaches, the CIP deviation typically:

options.label: Narrows
options.why: Balance-sheet capacity is withdrawn at reporting dates, so the arbitrage that closes the basis weakens.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The calendar pattern is the key evidence that the basis prices balance-sheet capacity.

working.label: Chain
working.display: Quarter end → banks shrink balance sheets → arbitrage capacity withdrawn → basis widens → normalises afterwards

takeaway: CIP deviations are a price for balance sheet, and they spike when balance sheet is scarcest, at quarter-ends.

reading: LR2025, Ch. 1: Liquidity Risk
setup: A firm has sold 5–10 year fixed-price oil supply contracts and hedges them with long, short-dated oil futures that are rolled forward and margined daily. Oil prices then fall sharply.
ask: Its near-term cash position:

options.label: Improves
options.why: The gain sits in the long-dated supply contracts and arrives only over years. The futures losses are paid in cash now.

options.label: Unaffected: the hedge is matched
options.why: It is matched in value but not in timing. The daily margin creates a cash-flow mismatch.

working.label: Futures leg
working.display: Long futures lose as oil falls → daily margin calls → cash out now

working.label: Contract leg
working.display: Fixed-price sales gain value, but the cash comes in over 5–10 years

takeaway: A value-matched hedge can still be a liquidity mismatch: short-dated margined hedges against long-dated exposures (Metallgesellschaft).

reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
setup: An exchange's order flow becomes dominated by positive feedback traders, who sell when prices fall and buy when prices rise.
ask: Market liquidity:

options.label: Improves
options.why: Positive feedback reinforces each move and makes the market one-sided. It is negative feedback traders who supply liquidity.

options.label: Unaffected
options.why: Trader type decides whether moves are absorbed or amplified.

working.label: Positive feedback
working.display: Sell into falls, buy into rises → moves reinforced → one-sided, unstable, illiquid

working.label: Negative feedback
working.display: Buy into falls, sell into rises → prices pulled back → liquid market

takeaway: Liquid markets are dominated by negative feedback traders. Positive feedback drains liquidity.
